title: Effect of warm rolling and heat treatment on heterogeneous austenite morphology and tensile property of 3Mn steel
abstract: Facing the current lack of clarity in temperature selection mechanisms for warm rolling in medium Mn steel, three warm rolling methods were conducted in 3Mn steel according to the rolling temperatures in the dual-phases region or ferrite region. Subsequently, the effect of heat treatment on the austenite morphologies and tensile properties of warm-rolling samples was studied. Rolling in dual-phase regions (750 °C) led to heterogeneous austenite morphology composed of equiaxed and lamellar grains while rolling in the ferrite region (600 °C) resulted in significant cementite precipitation and the absence of retained austenite. Warm rolling promoted the formation of dislocation cells in the lath-like grains, and they did not evolve into grain boundaries completely because low deformation temperature didn’t trigger the complete dynamic recrystallization. Tempering after rolling provided a significant enhancement in plasticity through the enrichment of C and Mn in austenite and the formation of multiple heterogeneous austenite morphologies with equiaxed, coarse lath-like and fine lamellar grains. In addition, superlattice structures in the matrix are formed through the formation of stacking fault networks and the spinodal decomposition. Ultimately, the exceptional properties were achieved in 3Mn steel, with an ultimate tensile strength of 1409 MPa and a total elongation of 27.3 %.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: As a representative material of the most promising advanced high-strength steel materials currently, medium Mn steel (3 – 12wt.%Mn) has gained significant attention due to its outstanding mechanical properties  [1,2] . With the development of heat treatment, a growing number of complex and effective heat treatment methods have been reported, including intercritical annealing-tempering (IAT), intercritical quenching-partitioning (IQ&P), flash annealing, and multiple annealing  [2–6] . These innovative heat treatment approaches promoted the effective application of the complex strengthening mechanisms, achieving the enrichment of C and Mn in austenite grains and even altering their sizes to form heterogeneous microstructures, thereby enhancing the stability of the austenite  [7–10] . These methods have been proven to be effective strategies for property strengthening  [3,11,12] .

However, it is gradually difficult to continue to improve the properties of medium Mn steel only relying on heat treatment  [6] . Moreover, compared to controlling grain size during heat treatment, pre-deformation is more effective in adjusting grain shape and size  [13] . Thus, as a typical pre-deformation method, warm rolling has been proposed for the rapid formation of multiple austenite morphologies and the construction of heterogeneous microstructure  [14] . Subsequently, C and Mn partitioning to austenite is achieved through heat treatment, thereby enhancing the stability of the austenite  [11,15,16] . Warm rolling, as a deformation process situated between hot rolling and cold rolling, combines the advantages of both methods  [17] . Compared to hot rolling, lower rolling temperatures cannot trigger complete dynamic recrystallization (DRX), and fine lath-like deformation grains are retained  [13,18] . Furthermore, warm rolling reduces the deformation resistance, allowing it to forego intermediate softening annealing compared to the cold rolling process for medium Mn steel with a higher martensite content  [19] . Hu et al.  [12]  conducted warm rolling on 7Mn steel and observed that, compared with the cold rolled microstructure that is usually completely recrystallized during intercritical annealing (IA), the warm rolled microstructure is just partially recrystallized due to the lower driving force that is accumulated. This leads to about 50 vol% of the retained austenite grains with both lamellar and equiaxed morphologies after IA, with the latter having a wide and almost evenly spaced size distribution. About 40 vol% of the retained austenite grains could sustainably transform to martensite during deformation because they had a range of mechanical stability owing to their different morphologies and wide size distributions. Zou et al.  [14]  found that hot rolling leads to annealed microstructures with a fully lamellar morphology. Through a dual-stage warm rolling process, a heterogeneous microstructure consisting of both lamellar and equiaxed grains was established, which induced the generation of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) and maintained the continuity of different structural regions. Under the influence of non-uniform stress, the heterogeneous microstructure enhanced strain-hardening capabilities, resulting in a significant improvement in tensile strength and excellent ductility. The establishment of this heterogeneous microstructure proves to be an effective approach in strengthening the microstructure and properties of medium Mn steel through warm rolling processes  [12,15,20] .

In the process of warm rolling, the steel needs to be heated and soaked at temperatures below the complete austenitization temperature A 3  for some time, followed by rolling. Generally, there are two distinct characteristic temperature regions in medium Mn steel below A 3 : dual-phase region (austenite and ferrite, temperature A 1  – A 3 ) and single-phase region (completely ferrite region, temperature below A 1 )  [21] . Thus, common combinations of soaking and rolling during warm rolling can be categorized into three states. In the first approach, both soaking and rolling are in the dual-phase region. The steel should be soaked in the dual-phase region for several minutes before every pass of rolling to ensure that the deformation temperature is always in the dual-phase region. The second state is direct warm rolling after soaking in the dual-phase region. It's worth noting in this state that the temperature of steel plates gradually decreases during the multi-pass warm rolling. Therefore, it is often overlooked by researchers that the deformation may occur in both dual-phase and single-phase regions due to the relatively narrow dual-phase region of low-Al medium Mn steel (usually between 650 °C and 800 °C)  [22–24] . In the third approach, both soaking and rolling are below the temperature A 1 , which doesn't involve the reverse transformation behavior of austenite. The unique phase transformation temperature region (A 1  ∼ A 3 ) for medium Mn steel adds complexity to the selection of warm rolling parameters. Therefore, when designing a warm rolling process for medium Mn steel, understanding microstructure evolution in different phase regions during warm rolling becomes critically important.

With the aforementioned objectives in mind, this paper systematically categorizes warm rolling methods. Three distinct warm rolling methods were applied to hot-rolled 3Mn steel, followed by heat treatment, and the influence of warm rolling in different temperature regions on the microstructure evolution and tensile properties was studied. Simultaneously, it elucidates the evolution mechanisms of heterogeneous austenite morphologies induced by warm rolling and heat treatment, which serves as a theoretical foundation for the selection of warm rolling schemes for medium Mn steel.

sections.heading: Experiment
paragraphs:
A 50 kg experimental steel ingot with a nominal chemical composition of 0.38C-3.14Mn-0.43Al-1.64Si-0.048Nb-0.24Cr-0.15Mo-Fe (wt%) was cast in a vacuum induction furnace. After holding at 1200 °C for 1.5 h, the ingot was hot forged into slabs of 80 mm × 40 mm in section size and then was air-cooled to room temperature. Subsequently, the forged slabs were soaked at 1200 °C for 2 h, and then were hot-rolled to a plate with a thickness of 6 mm in the temperature range of 1150 ∼ 950 °C. After air cooling to 650 °C and holding for 1 h, the slabs were air-cooled to room temperature to simulate the coiling process of hot-rolled steel. The phase property diagram is calculated by the software Thermo-Calc with the TCFE10 database. Austenite transformation temperatures A 1  and A 3  of experimental steel were measured through a thermal dilatometer (DIL805A). For hot-rolled plates, there are three different treatment routes of warm rolling: both soaking and rolling in the dual-phase region, soaking in the dual-phase region followed by rolling in the ferrite region, and both soaking and rolling in the ferrite region, which are named WR-1, WR-2, and WR-3, respectively. The selected temperatures for the dual-phase region and ferrite region were 750 °C and 600 °C, respectively, according to the temperatures A 1  and A 3 . Then, WR-1 was tempered at 400 °C for 10 min and the tempered sample was named WR1-T. WR-2 and WR-3 were annealed at 725 °C for 10 min, followed by water quenching, and the annealing samples were named WR2-IA and WR3-IA, respectively. The routes of warm rolling and heat treatments are shown in  Fig. 1 
                      .

All tensile tests were conducted on the tensile specimens (3 mm in thickness, 6 mm in width, 25 mm in gauge length, and 80 mm in total length) at an initial strain rate of 0.001 s −1  at room temperature using a universal tensile test machine (MTS Exceed E45). Strain is acquired based on the measurement result of an extensometer that tracks the entire deformation process. The strain value is the ratio of the measured value of the extensometer to the gauge length (25 mm). The tensile sample is sampled from the middle of the warm rolled plate after heat treatment, the tensile direction is the rolling direction, and the thickness of the sample is the thickness of the plate. Each sample is tested three times, and the middle value is recognized as the effective value. The microstructures were observed using a field-emission scanning electronic microscope (FE-SEM; ZEISS Gemini 500) equipped with an electron backscattered diffractometer (EBSD, Symmetry S2), a field-emission transmission electron microscope (FE-TEM, JEOL2100, 200 kV) with an energy-dispersive spectroscope (EDS) and a Spherical aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy (AC-TEM, Titan ETEM G2, 300 kV). The volume fraction of retained austenite was calculated by the integrated intensities of the diffraction reflections including the (2 0 0)α, (2 1 1)α, (2 0 0)γ, (2 2 0)γ, and (3 1 1)γ peaks measured through X-ray diffraction (XRD, smartLab)  [9] . The XRD tests were performed with a scan range from 47° to 93° and a scan rate of 2°/min using an X-ray diffractometer with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 Å)  [25,26] . XRD patterns and results are listed in  Fig. S1  in the  supplementary file . The samples for EBSD observation were polished using a suspension including 2.5 μm diamond particles and then were electro-polished at 20 V for 25 s using a mixed solution of 90 % ethyl alcohol and 10 % perchloric acid to remove the layer damaged by mechanical polishing. The accelerating voltage, working distance, probe current, and step size for the EBSD operation were 20 kV, 17 ∼ 20 mm, 15nA, and 80 nm, respectively. The obtained EBSD data were calculated by the software AZtecCrystal to obtain the fitting ellipse sizes of grains. Thin foil samples for TEM observation were prepared by mechanical polishing down to ∼ 30 μm in thickness followed by further thinning was accomplished using an ion thinning instrument (Gatan691). Transmission Kikuchi Diffraction (TKD) analysis of TEM samples was conducted using EBSD to obtain synchronized orientation and phase distribution analysis of the TEM microstructure.

sections.heading: Results
paragraphs:
Fig. 2 
                      (a) and (b) present the phase property diagram and the value of A 1  and A 3  measured through a thermal dilatometer. The calculated A 1  and A 3  in  Fig. 2 (a) are 697 °C and 800 °C, respectively, which closely matched the experimental results in  Fig. 2 (b). A lamellar microstructure is exhibited in hot-rolled samples in  Fig. 2 (c–d) and the original austenite grain boundaries marked as white dotted lines are still clearly visible. The calculated precipitation temperature region of M 3 C is 350℃∼720℃. Thus, there may be M 3 C precipitated during warm rolling.

These three warm rolling methods are primarily designed to compare the effects on microstructure and tensile properties when soaking and rolling temperatures fall within different phase regions during the entire process of warm rolling.  Fig. 3 
                       and  Fig. 4 
                       display SEM and EBSD microstructure of the three warm-rolled samples. The microstructure of WR-1 exhibits distinct heterogeneous morphologies consisting of lamellar and equiaxed grains and the carbides are mainly distributed on the equiaxed grains. Moreover, some adjacent equiaxed grains are still maintained within the lath-like boundaries. The inverse pole figure (IPF) in  Fig. 4 (d) reveals that these equiaxed grains within the same lath-like boundaries share the same orientation.  Fig. 4 (b) and (c) show that WR-2 and WR-3 also exhibit large lamellar grains and fine equiaxed grains. As the same as WR-1, adjacent fine equiaxed grains maintain similar orientations within the same lath-like boundaries, which is related to incomplete DRX. In addition, more precipitation of more carbides was also exhibited in WR-2 and WR-3. According to the predicted results from the phase property diagram, the carbides in warm-rolled samples are identified as cementite (M 3 C). Meanwhile, TEM results in  Fig. S2  of the  supplementary file  also prove that the carbides are M 3 C particles. The isothermal and rolling temperatures for WR-1 are close to the temperature of cementite dissolution according to  Fig. 2 (b), with fewer cementite precipitates in WR-1 than in the other two samples.  Fig. 4 (g–h) depicts the DRX state of the three experimental steels. WR-1, rolled at a higher temperature, exhibits the highest degree of DRX. In contrast, WR-2 exhibits the lowest degree of recrystallization.

EBSD results in  Fig. 4  demonstrate that only WR-1 has austenite, with an austenite content of 22 vol%, while WR-2 and WR-3 have no retained austenite. XRD analysis of the three samples, as shown in  Fig. S1 , reveals that the austenite content in WR-1, WR-2, and WR-3 is 19.0 vol%, 0 vol% and 0 vol%, respectively, which is similar to the EBSD results. This indicates the significance of rolling temperature in determining the austenite content in warm-rolled microstructures. The purpose of heat treatment in medium Mn steel is to introduce and stabilize the austenite, thereby utilizing the TRIP effect of the austenite to enhance strain hardening during deformation and delay plastic failure. WR-1 already contains 19.0 vol% of austenite, so the heat treatment for WR-1 does not need to re-introduce austenite through intercritical annealing any longer. Instead, it underwent a heat treatment at 400 °C for 10 min to enhance the stability of the existing austenite, and then WR1-T was acquired. For WR-2 and WR-3 without austenite, intercritical annealing at 725 °C for 10 min was employed to introduce the austenite. Thus, the introduction of austenite in WR1-T occurred during warm rolling, while WR-2 and WR-3 had no austenite in their final microstructure and could only acquire austenite through intercritical annealing. Comparing these two cases allows for an assessment of the impact of introducing austenite at different stages on tensile properties. The final microstructures after heat treatment are shown in  Fig. 5 
                      .

The phase contents, grain sizes, carbide sizes, and GNDs density of WR and WR-T are listed in  Table 1 
                       based on the XRD, TEM, and EBSD results in  Figs. S1–S5  of the  supplementary material . According to  Table 1 , the content of austenite increased through the heat treatments. The fraction of austenite increased from 19.0 ± 2.5 vol% in WR-1 to 21.2 ± 3.5 vol% in WR-T, and the austenite contents in WR2-IA and WR3-IA are 13.9 ± 1.8 vol% and 21.6 ± 3.1 vol%, respectively. The average size (expressed in average grain diameter, μm) of austenite grains increases from 0.54 ± 0.04 μm in WR-1 to 0.62 ± 0.07 μm in WR1-T, and the average sizes of austenite grains in WR2-IA and WR3-IA are 0.60 ± 0.03 μm and 0.64 ± 0.03 μm, respectively. Not only does the size of austenite grains increase, but the average size of BCC grains also increases. The heterogeneous morphologies were continuously maintained in WR1-T, while the microstructure of WR2-IA and WR3-IA is predominantly composed of equiaxed grains. After heat treatment, GNDs density in WR1 is not decrease, while that in WR2 and WR3 decreases obviously. Annealing effectively promotes grain recovery and recrystallization of WR2 and WR3, while tempering does not seem to affect the GNDs density of WR-1.

Fig. 6 
                       depicts the mechanical curves for the samples of warm rolling and heat treatment. WR-1 exhibited continuous yielding behavior during tensile testing, but after tempering, obvious yield plateaus and slight stress serrations occurred. The yield plateau is evident in plastic instability behavior, which is often observed in medium Mn steel. In contrast to WR-1, WR-2, and WR-3 displayed distinct yield plateaus. However, after annealing, WR2-IA and WR3-IA exhibited continuous yielding behavior, and plastic instability behavior represented by the yield plateau disappeared.

Table 2 
                       presents the properties of the samples after warm rolling and heat treatment. In warm rolling samples, WR-1 exhibited the lowest yield strength (YS) and the highest ultimate tensile strength (UTS), and three steels had similar total elongation (TE), approximately 15 %. After heat treatment, the tensile properties of WR1-T showed a significant improvement. Although the strength decreased from 1725 ± 10 MPa to 1409 ± 4 MPa, the elongation increased from 15.0 ± 2.8 % to 27.3 ± 1.8 %, and the product of strength and elongation (PSE) rose from 25.9GPa·% to 38.2GPa·%, which is exceptional for 3Mn steel. However, for WR2 and WR3, annealing did not lead to a significant property improvement. In contrast to WR2 and WR3, in which austenite was reintroduced through annealing after warm rolling, WR1 introduced austenite during the warm rolling. Introducing and retaining austenite during the warm rolling stage is more favorable for enhancing the tensile properties of medium Mn steel. Therefore, conducting the entire process of warm rolling in the dual-phase region appears to be the optimal warm rolling approach for medium Mn steel.

sections.heading: Microstructure evolution during warm rolling and heat treatments
paragraphs:
TKD analysis in  Fig. 7 
                          provides more detailed insights into the microstructure of the three warm-rolled samples.  Fig. 7 (a 1 –a 4 ) shows elongated BCC grains and lamellar microstructure of matensite/austenite (M/A).  Fig. 7 (a 3 ) shows the distribution of GNDs density. Martensite possesses more dislocation density than ferrite. The elongated BCC grains with lower GNDs density are the deformed ferrite structure. There is a higher dislocation density in BCC grains within the lamellar microstructure of BCC + FCC in the white dashed circle of  Fig. 7 (a 2 ), which further proves that this BCC is martensite. For WR-2 and WR-3, the microstructure still shows clearly elongated outlines of the deformation grains. The retain for the elongated lamellar microstructure is because DRX was not fully triggered. During complete DRX, grains undergo re-nucleation in the form of dislocation cells in the elongated lamellar grains induced by tensile deformation, and dislocation cells would continue to grow to form sub-grains until entire grains. As shown in  Fig. 7 (b) and (c), the presence of dislocation cell structures is evident within the lamellar outlines in the WR-2 and WR-3 microstructures, and even some lamellar outlines have already formed multiple equiaxed grains, which are indicative of the local initiation of DRX.

Warm rolling can introduce internal stresses within grains and promote the formation of complex defects. High-resolution TEM images in  Fig. 8 
                          provide a clear view of the defect structures within warm-rolled grains. In WR-1, a significant number of intersecting fault dislocations are generated within the austenite grains. These fault dislocations show dislocation intersections on the plane [1 1 0], forming fault dislocation networks, which resulted in a superlattice structure due to internal distortion and the generation of satellite spots around the main diffraction spots  [27,28] . The Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT) to the satellite spots could reveal the distribution of superlattice structure, as shown in  Fig. 8 (a 4 ). There is a strong correlation between the superlattice structure distribution and the stacking fault network. The existence of stacking fault networks can cause the accumulation of dislocations in the process of deformation, which plays a significant role in the work hardening of materials  [29,30] . The satellite spots are not only found in austenite but are also observed in the ferrite, as depicted in  Fig. 8 (b). The recovery and DRX during warm rolling are not complete, resulting in a large number of dislocations or defects inside the grains and forming a locally ordered phase structure, which leads to the formation of satellite spots. At the same time, these defects also lead to the enrichment of elements and the formation of spinodal decomposition microstructure alternately precipitated by C and Mn. Spinodal decomposition is a common cause of satellite spots  [31] . In  Fig. 8 (d 1 ), it is observed that solute atoms segregate at dislocations in the ferrite of WR-3 through a high-angle annular dark-field image. In  Fig. 8 (c), it is observed that nano-sized M 7 C 3  particles precipitate within the matrix, which is also related to the enrichment of elements at the defects. The element enrichment in the defects satisfies the nucleation condition of M 7 C 3 . Lamellar defects in the M 3 C carbides were observed through high-resolution TEM in  Fig. 8 (d 2 –d 4 ). It was found that M 3 C carbides with lamellar defects also led to the presence of a partial superlattice structure, as shown in  Fig. 8 (d 4 ). Obviously, different from the formation mechanism of the locally ordered phase in the matrix, the satellite spots caused by the layered ordered phase of carbides are attributed to the precipitation and growth of carbides affected by warm rolling.

Fig. 9  illustrates the heterogeneous microstructure of WR1-T, including larger-sized lath-like and finer-sized lamellar austenite grains, which is consistent with the EBSD characterization results shown in  Fig. 5 . According to the TEM-EDS results in  Table 3 , tempering increases the C and Mn content in austenite, and fined lamellar austenite exhibits higher Mn content than coursing lath-like austenite with minimal differences in carbon content, which indicates that lamellar austenite exhibits higher chemical stability. Grain boundary migration is the primary factor for the increase in content and variation in morphologies of austenite during tempering  [32] . Austenite absorbs Mn and C from surrounding martensite and ferrite during tempering, with the migration of grain boundaries towards martensite or ferrite, resulting in increased size and content of austenite and forming coarse lath-like austenite grains  [33] . Fine lamellar austenite primarily originates from martensitic transformation, possibly during warm rolling or tempering. For M/A before tempering, a large number of solute atoms and dislocations within martensite limit grain boundary migration of lamellar austenite, elevating Mn and C content in grains without altering size. When austenite surrounds ferrite with low Mn, there is a new low Mn region near boundaries in austenite after grain migration. The diffusion of Mn from the original austenite area towards the low Mn regions leads to a decrease in average Mn content in austenite and the coursing lath-like austenite grains form when diffusion is complete. Thus, incomplete Mn diffusion would result in the transformation of austenite with low Mn regions back into the BCC phase during cooling, retaining the Mn-enriched lamellar austenite.  Fig. 9 (e) shows sub-grain boundaries in coarse lath-like austenite formed by dislocation entanglements, which is indicative of tempering-induced grain recovery, while no sub-grain boundaries are observed in lamellar austenite. Sub-grain boundaries affect austenite stability unfavorably by inducing stress concentration during deformation, which would promote TRIP effects in advance. Meanwhile, Although tempering could eliminated part of dislocations, the occurence of fine lamellar austenite and M/A also could increase the GNDs density. Thus, there is almost no variation in the GNDs density before and after tempering in WR-1 as shown in  Table 1 .

For WR-2 and WR-3, austenite introduction is achieved through intercritical annealing and the enrichment level of C and Mn in austenite is lower than that in WR1-T. During annealing, the reverse transformation happened in martensite and austenite nucleated on grain boundaries and carbides, leading to the predominance of equiaxed grains in the newly nucleated austenite.  Fig. 10  analyzes the austenite morphology and orientation changes in WR2-IA.  Fig. 10 (b) displays the diffraction spots of austenite and there are also other darker satellite spots around the main spot, which indicates that the nanoscale structures formed during warm rolling have a hereditary influence after heat treatment.

TEM and TKD have captured a structure similar to the M/A microstructure in WR3-IA, as shown by the regions enclosed by the black dashed lines in  Fig. 11 (c). The formation of M/A structures is related to the phase transformation of the original austenite grains. When original austenite grains undergo martensitic transformation, the transformation occurs first from within the austenite, and some austenite is retained near the grain boundaries. This is because the grain boundaries have higher defect density and store a higher content of Mn and C elements, making this portion of the austenite more stable. Compared to the common M/A microstructure,  Fig. 11 (b) shows that a special mixed structure of BCC and FCC was found, in which BCC was σ-Fe and FCC was still austenite. Dark-field images in  Fig. 11 (b) show the distribution of σ-Fe and austenite.                           FCC. The formation of σ-Fe is not commonly observed in medium Mn steel and is more typical in dual-phase stainless steel  [34–36] . Previous research suggests that σ-Fe typically forms in the range of 650–950 °C. The formation mechanism of σ-Fe is primarily related to eutectoid transformations, where ferrite decomposes into σ-Fe and secondary austenite  [37,38] . The enrichment of Cr and Mo is a primary factor inducing the appearance of σ-Fe, which usually nucleates at the grain boundaries of both austenite and ferrite. This suggests a new nucleation mechanism during the warm rolling and annealing process, which provides high defect density regions that favor the enrichment of Cr and Mo. This enables the transformation of ferrite into σ-Fe during the annealing process. σ-Fe is the most harmful precipitate phase, being hard and brittle, which significantly reduces the plasticity  [39] .

sections.heading: Strengthening of multiple heterogeneous austenite morphologies on tensile properties
paragraphs: Warm rolling has effectively restructured the phase composition, grain size, and morphology in medium Mn steel. Austenite is a critical strengthening phase in medium Mn steel and its stability is influenced by composition and size  [16,40] . Traditional research on medium Mn steel has often focused on the impact of austenite content on mechanical properties. Based on the XRD results, although WR1-T and WR3-IA have similar austenite content, WR1-T exhibits higher tensile properties. While it varies significantly in the austenite content between WR2-IA and WR3-IA, their tensile properties are essentially the same. Austenite content is no longer the primary factor affecting tensile properties in warm rolling samples. On the one hand, as shown by the TEM-EDS results in  Table 3 , warm rolling in the dual-phase region and tempering gave more C and Mn content partitioning into austenite, which greatly enhances the chemistry stability of austenite. On the other hand, the morphology distribution of austenite grains is also important for the tensile properties of medium Mn steel. There are obvious heterogeneous morphologies consisting of lamellar + equiaxed austenite grains in WR-1, so it is necessary to further characterize the morphology distribution of austenite in the heat-treated samples.

Multiple EBSD observations for each sample are conducted, obtaining statistical data for the size or morphology distribution of 200 austenite grains in various random areas.  Fig. 12 
                         (a) shows one set of the austenite grain distribution for WR1, WR1-T, WR2-IA, and WR3-IA. Tempering significantly results in grains coarsening and the shapes of austenite in WR2-IA and WR3-IA are mainly equiaxed. Each austenite grain is fitted into an elliptical shape because both equiaxed and lath-like grains could be described in elliptical shape.                             a/b 
                          in 1.6 ∼ 1.8, 2.4 ∼ 2.8, and above 4 represents the grains with equiaxed, coarse lath-like, and lamellar shape, respectively. Tempering not only increases austenite content and grain size but also significantly enhances the heterogeneity distribution of austenite grains, forming multiple heterogeneous austenite morphologies, which are distinguished in equiaxed grains, coarse lath-like grains, and fine lamellar austenite.

The establishment of multiple heterostructures induces the appearance of an ordered TRIP effect. In the process of deformation, the TRIP effect first occurs in the coarse lath-like austenite with low stability, which provides the work hardening of the early deformation. Subsequently, martensite transformation would be triggered in equiaxed austenite grains. The fine lamellar austenite with the highest stability would provide a TRIP effect in the later stage of deformation, which could delay the initiation or propagation of cracks and further improve the plasticity. Compared with WR1-T, coarser equiaxed austenite grains are exhibited in WR2-IA and WR3-IA because annealing leads to more substantial martensite reversion and recrystallization.  Fig. 12 (c) reveals that the values of  
                            a/b 
                          for WR2-IA and WR3-IA are mainly below 2.0, indicating equiaxed grains as their dominant feature.  Fig. 12 (a) also shows that WR2-IA and WR3-IA have larger grain sizes. Coarsening equiaxed austenite grains possess lower stability. During the initial stages of deformation, these large equiaxed grains undergo the TRIP effect, enhancing work hardening rates, and thus not displaying a yield plateau. However, the lack of more stable austenite leads to reduced TRIP effect in the later stages, unable to further delay the onset of plastic cracking, which results in lower ductility.

Fig. 13 
                          illustrates the work-hardening curves of the samples after warm rolling or heat treatment. In WR-1, the work hardening rate decreases continuously, attributed to the effective control of the TRIP effect during deformation by heterogeneous austenite structure. However, WR-2 and WR-3 show almost no work hardening ability due to the absence of austenite, resulting in the lack of TRIP effect during deformation. After IA introduces austenite in WR2-IA and WR3-IA, continuous work-hardening behavior was exhibited, which highlighted the crucial role of the TRIP effect in achieving work-hardening ability. Despite the enhanced plasticity from the establishment of multiple heterogeneous austenite microstructures in WR1-T, continuous work hardening ability during deformation was not achieved. This is attributed to the intermittent triggering of the TRIP effect during deformation caused by the multiple heterogeneous austenite grains with different stability. Therefore, the establishment of multiple heterogeneous microstructures in austenite should consider the continuity of the TRIP effect during deformation, which should be further explored in subsequent research.

Through the study of the three warm rolling and heat treatment approaches, the morphology and microstructure of austenite emerge as the primary determinants of the exceptional properties of 3Mn steel. Based on prior investigations concentrating on constructing a morphology of lamellar and equiaxed heterogeneity, the presence of multiple heterogeneous morphologies characterized by equiaxed, coarse lath-like, and fine lamellar grains significantly enhances the mechanical properties.  Fig. 14 
                          compares the tensile properties of the WR1-T with data from previous studies on medium Mn steels. Compared with medium Mn steel with higher Mn content (5 ∼ 12Mn), the experimental steel can achieve similar tensile properties under the condition of 3Mn, which also proves the significance of this work. Compared with medium Mn steel with similar Mn content (3 ∼ 5Mn, PSE is mainly at 20 ∼ 30 GPa·%), the PSE of 3Mn steel in this work is close to 40GPa·%. In addition, compared with the 3 ∼ 5Mn steel with similar PSE, the strength and plasticity of WR1-T have an excellent strong-plastic match, the UTS is up to 1400 MPa, and the TE is more than 25 %.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
This work presents a comparative study of three warm rolling and elaborates on the effect of warm rolling and heat treatment on tensile properties. Finally, the following conclusions are drawn: 
                         
                            (1) 
                            DRX is suppressed during warm rolling and the grain morphologies mainly exhibit deformation-induced elongated shapes. Rolling in a dual-phase temperature region induces the retention of austenite and the formation of heterogeneous austenite morphologies consisting of equiaxed and lamellar grains. Conversely, rolling within the ferrite region results in the absence of retained austenite. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            Tempering after warm rolling in the dual-phase region not only enhances the content and stability of austenite but also stimulates the formation of multiple heterogeneous austenite morphologies, including equiaxed, coarsening lath-like, and fine lamellar austenite grains. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            The formation of superlattice structures in austenite and ferrite/martensite is attributed to the construction of stacking fault networks and the spinodal decomposition, respectively, during warm rolling and heat treatments. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            Compared ferrite region, warm rolling in the dual-phase region and tempering is the best method to enhance the tensile properties through the construction of multiple heterogeneous austenite morphologies, and ultimately, UTS of 1409 MPa and TE of 27.3 % are achieved in 3Mn steel.
